Figures 73 and 74 illustrates the load-displacement curves for the ‘along’ and ‘across’ specimens. The data is very repeatable. For the along specimens there is some modulus variation, attributed to areas of high preferred fiber orientation (location where specimen is cut). The typical failure modes in flexure for constituent SMC and TCF with over molded SMC are shown in Figure 75. The key difference was that failure initiated at the tensile side of the constituent SMC and progressed up in a shear direction. For the TCF over molded SMC, the failure was resisted by the TCF and initiates a few layers above the TCF. This failure is not at the interface between TCF and SMC, but in the bulk SMC 2-3 layers above the TCF and propagates transversely. Failure modes in flexure of the (above) constituent SMC and (below) TCF with over molded SMC 56 More Studies with Recycled Carbon Fiber Mats One of the goals of the work was to produce SMC using recycled carbon fibers (rCF). Since the source of rCF is primarily from pyrolysis, shredding, solvolysis and thermolysis, continuous CF is typically converted to discontinuous CF. Companies such as ELG, Vartega, Carbon Conversion Solutions (CCS) have proprietary processes to convert the CF into roll good such as non-woven discontinuous mats of 36 to 50” width. Recycled carbon fiber mats-composites mechanical testing In this work through partnership with ELG and CCS we procured rCF roll good mats. One aspect of the study was to evaluate the mechanical properties of these mats on a constituent basis. For this work the mats were processed using low viscosity epoxy resin via vacuum infusion and the infused panel(s) were subjected to compression molding to obtain higher consolidation, Figure 77. The goal was to obtain higher performing material, hence the choice of epoxy over vinyl ester for these studies. Figure 76 illustrates the rCF materials as sourced from ELG and CCS respectively. The ELG uses a pyrolysis process, wet laid and stitch bonding to produce the mats. The CCS uses pyrolysis and air laid process to produce the mats. The mats have a nominal 200 gsm aerial weight. They come in rolls of 48-50” wide. Figure 76 illustrates the steps of converting the rCF mats into composite panels using the vacuum infusion-compression molding processing steps. Coupons were extracted to measure tensile and flexural properties. A compression molding only process was adopted in some cases to produce rCF-PA6 plates (this data is not reported here).
